name: Japanese
notes: Start with hiragana — it is a true alphabet of 46 sounds and can be learned in a week. Once you can read it, everything else in Japanese becomes approachable. Japanese has no tones and very regular pronunciation, which makes speaking it far easier than reading it.
syllabus: Both kana in full, 110 kanji (the whole JLPT N5 kanji list), and about 760 words and phrases — the whole JLPT N5 vocabulary (around 800 words), plus the everyday set phrases. N5 is the first of five official levels; passing it means simple, slow conversations. Grammar is in the sentence-patterns deck and the guide. Cards can be spoken aloud if Windows has a Japanese voice installed. Next: N4 (another 700 words and 170 kanji).
